label: ex:motivating
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:motivating} Consider the positively weighted graph $G$ with vertex set $\{1,2,3,4,5\}$, edge set \[ E = \bigl\{ \{1,2\},\{1,4\},\{1,5\},\{2,3\} \bigr\}, \] and unit edge weights. Its Laplacian is 
\[ L_G = \begin{bmatrix} 3&-1&0&-1&-1\\ -1&2&-1&0&0\\ 0&-1&1&0&0\\ -1&0&0&1&0\\ -1&0&0&0&1 \end{bmatrix}. \] 
The eigenvalue $\lambda=1$ is simple, with $E_1(L_G)=\operatorname{span}\{y\}$, where \[ y= \begin{bmatrix} 0\\0\\0\\1\\-1 \end{bmatrix}. \] 
Let \(H\) be the graph with the same vertex set as \(G\), edge set
\(\{\{1,3\}\}\), and edge weight \(\omega>0\).  Let $b=e_1-e_3$, $\Omega=[\omega]$, and $X_{\Omega}=\sqrt{\omega}\,b$. Then 
\[ L_{G+H}= L_G+\omega bb^T = \begin{bmatrix} 3+\omega&-1&-\omega&-1&-1\\ -1&2&-1&0&0\\ -\omega&-1&1+\omega&0&0\\ -1&0&0&1&0\\ -1&0&0&0&1 \end{bmatrix}. \] 
Since $b^Ty=0$, we have $L_{G+H} y=L_Gy=y$. Thus, $y$ is an inherited $1$-eigenvector of $L_{G+H}$ for every $\omega>0$. Now consider \[ \widetilde y = \begin{bmatrix} 0\\-1\\-1\\1\\1 \end{bmatrix}. \] A direct calculation gives $L_G\widetilde y=\widetilde y-b$ and $b^T\widetilde y=1$. Consequently, $L_{G+H}\widetilde y=\widetilde y+(\omega-1)b$, and therefore $L_{G+H}\widetilde y=\widetilde y$ if and only if $\omega=1$. In fact, we can show that 
\[ E_1(L_{G+H}) = \begin{cases} \operatorname{span}\{y\},&\omega\neq1,\\[1mm] \operatorname{span}\{y,\widetilde y\},&\omega=1. \end{cases} \] Thus, inheritance occurs for every $\omega>0$, whereas emergence occurs only at the exceptional weight $\omega=1$. At this value, the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $1$ increases from $1$ to $2$: the direction spanned by $y$ is inherited, while the direction spanned by $\widetilde y$ is emergent. Moreover, every vector $\alpha y+\beta\widetilde y$ with $\beta\neq0$ is an emergent $1$-eigenvector of $L_{G+H}$.
head: environment
name: Weight-dependent emergence after adding a new edge

label: ex:emergence-existing-edge
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:emergence-existing-edge} Consider the positively weighted graph $G$ with vertex set $\{1,2,3,4\}$, edge set \[ E = \bigl\{ \{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{1,4\},\{2,3\} \bigr\},\] 
and unit edge weights.
Let $L_G$ be its Laplacian. A direct calculation gives $\sigma(L_G)=\{0,1,3,4\}$, $E_4(L_G)=\operatorname{span}\{y\}$, where \[ y= \begin{bmatrix} -3\\1\\1\\1 \end{bmatrix}, \] and  \(E_3(L_G)=\operatorname{span}\{\widetilde y\}\), where \[ \widetilde y = \begin{bmatrix} 0\\-1\\1\\0 \end{bmatrix}. \] 

Let $H$ be the graph with the same vertex set as $G$, edge set $\{\{2,3\}\}$, and edge weight $\omega>0$. Note that the edge $\{2,3\}$ is already present in $G$. Let $b=e_2-e_3$, $\Omega=[\omega]$, and $L_{G+H}=L_G+\omega bb^T$. Since \(b^Ty=0\), we have
\[
L_{G+H}y
=
L_Gy+\omega b(b^Ty)
=
L_Gy
=
4y.
\]
Thus, \(y\) is an inherited \(4\)-eigenvector for every \(\omega>0\). On the other hand, \(b=-\widetilde y\), and hence
\(
bb^T\widetilde y=2\widetilde y.
\)
Therefore,
\[
L_{G+H}\widetilde y
=
L_G\widetilde y+\omega bb^T\widetilde y
=
(3+2\omega)\widetilde y.
\]

Because \(L_G\) is symmetric, eigenspaces corresponding to distinct
eigenvalues are orthogonal. Since \(b\) spans \(E_3(L_G)\), every vector
\(z\) in \(E_0(L_G)\), \(E_1(L_G)\), or \(E_4(L_G)\) satisfies
\(b^Tz=0\). Hence,
\[
L_{G+H}z
=
L_Gz+\omega b(b^Tz)
=
L_Gz.
\]
Thus, all eigenvectors of \(L_G\) corresponding to the eigenvalues
\(0\), \(1\), and \(4\) remain eigenvectors of \(L_{G+H}\) with the
same eigenvalues. The only original eigendirection affected by the
update is the direction spanned by \(\widetilde y\), whose eigenvalue
changes from \(3\) to \(3+2\omega\).
Consequently,
\[
E_4(L_{G+H})
=
\begin{cases}
\operatorname{span}\{y\},&\omega\neq\frac12,\\[1mm]
\operatorname{span}\{y,\widetilde y\},&\omega=\frac12.
\end{cases}
\]
Therefore, \(y\) is inherited for every \(\omega>0\), whereas emergence
occurs only when \(\omega=1/2\). At that value, \(\widetilde y\) is an
emergent \(4\)-eigenvector.

This shows that emergence can occur by increasing the weight of an  existing edge, without adding a new edge to the graph. 
The example also shows that an emergent $\lambda$-eigenvector need not be a completely new eigendirection of the original Laplacian: $\widetilde y$ is already an eigenvector of $L_G$, but for the different eigenvalue $3$. 
In general, however, an emergent eigenvector may have components in several eigenspaces of $L_G$.
head: environment
name: Weight-dependent emergence after increasing the weight of an existing edge

label: thm:inheritance-emergence-dichotomy
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:inheritance-emergence-dichotomy} Let $\lambda\in\sigma(L_G)$ and suppose that  $0
eq y\in E_\lambda(L_{G+H})$. Then \(y\) is inherited if and only if \(X_\Omega^Ty=0\), or,
equivalently, \(B^Ty=0\). Hence, \(y\) is emergent if and only if
\(X_\Omega^Ty
eq0\), or, equivalently, \(B^Ty
eq0\).
head: environment
name: Inheritance--emergence dichotomy

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that $X_\Omega^T y=0$. Since $L_{G+H}=L_G+X_\Omega X_\Omega^T$ and $L_{G+H} y=\lambda y$, we obtain \[ (L_G-\lambda I_n)y = (L_{G+H}-\lambda I_n)y-X_\Omega (X_\Omega^Ty)  = 0. \] Thus, $y\in E_\lambda(L_G)$, and hence $y$ is inherited.
 
 Conversely, suppose that $y$ is inherited. Then $L_Gy=L_{G+H} y=\lambda y$, so $X_\Omega X_\Omega^Ty=(L_{G+H}-L_G)y=0$. Since $\ker(X_{\Omega}X_{\Omega}^T)= \ker (X_{\Omega}^T)$, we have $X_{\Omega}^Ty=0$.  Finally, since $X_\Omega^T=\Omega^{1/2}B^T$ and $\Omega^{1/2}$ is invertible, we have $X_\Omega^Ty=0$ if and only if $B^Ty=0$. This completes the proof of the characterization of inherited eigenvectors.
 
 The characterization of emergent eigenvectors is the negation of the inherited condition for a nonzero vector in $E_\lambda(L_{G+H})$.
head: environment

label: lem:inherited-eigenvectors
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{lem:inherited-eigenvectors}
Let \(\lambda\in\sigma(L_{G})\). For \(0\neq y\in E_\lambda(L_{G+H})\), the following
statements are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\rm(i)]  \(y\) is inherited.

\item[\rm(ii)] 
\(y\in\ker(B^T)\); that is, \(y_i=y_j\) for every update edge
\(\{i,j\}\in F\).

\item[\rm(iii)] The entries of \(y\) are constant on each connected
component of \(H\).
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Inherited eigenvectors

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $X_{\Omega}^Ty=0$ if and only if $B^Ty=0$, the equivalence of (i) and (ii) follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:inheritance-emergence-dichotomy}.

The entries of \(y\) agree at the endpoints of every update edge if and only if 
they agree along every path in the update graph (that is,  \(y\) is constant
on each connected component of \(H\)). 
This proves the equivalence of \emph{(ii)} and
\emph{(iii)}.
head: environment

label: thm:inherited-eigenspace
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: The inherited eigenspace

title: Proof
body_md:
The first and second characterizations of $\mathcal{U}_{\lambda}$ in \eqref{eq:inherited-space-characterizations}  follow from Theorem \ref{thm:inheritance-emergence-dichotomy} and Proposition  \ref{lem:inherited-eigenvectors}, respectively. The third equality in \eqref{eq:inherited-space-characterizations} follows since    every vector in \(E_\lambda(L_G)\) has the
form \(Q_\lambda a\) for a unique \(a\in\mathbb R^m\), and  $Q_{\lambda}$ has full column rank. 

The equivalence of (i) and (ii) follows from the last characterization of $\mathcal{U}_{\lambda}$ in \eqref{eq:inherited-space-characterizations} taking into account that  $Q_\lambda$ has full column rank.

Finally, let $A:=\Omega^{1/2}B^TQ_\lambda$.
Then
\[
Q_\lambda^TB\Omega B^TQ_\lambda
=
\bigl(\Omega^{1/2}B^TQ_{\lambda}\bigr)^T
\bigl(\Omega^{1/2}B^TQ_{\lambda}\bigr)
=
A^TA.
\]
Since $\Omega^{1/2}$ is invertible, $A$ has full column rank if and only if $B^TQ_\lambda$ has full column rank. Moreover, $A^TA$ is nonsingular if and only if $A$ has full column rank. This justifies the equivalence of
\textup{(ii)} and \textup{(iii)}.
head: environment

label: cor:inherited-dimension
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Dimension and preservation through inheritance

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $Q_{\lambda}$ has orthonormal columns, the map $a\mapsto Q_{\lambda}a$ is injective.
Therefore, by \eqref{eq:inherited-space-characterizations},
\(
\dim\mathcal U_\lambda=\dim\ker(B^TQ_{\lambda}).
\)
The rank--nullity theorem gives
\eqref{eq:inherited-dimension}.

Finally, if \(p<m_\lambda(L_G)\), then
\(
\operatorname{rank}(B^TQ_\lambda)\leq p<m_\lambda(L_G).
\)
It follows from \eqref{eq:inherited-dimension} that
\(\dim\mathcal U_\lambda>0\), so \(\lambda\) is preserved through
inheritance.
head: environment

label: rem:inheritance-weight-independence
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:inheritance-weight-independence}
For a fixed set \(F\) of updated edges, the inherited eigenspace
$\mathcal U_\lambda$, and therefore its dimension, is independent of
the positive update weights in $\Omega$.
This contrasts with emergence, which may depend on \(\Omega\), as shown in
Examples~\ref{ex:motivating} and~\ref{ex:emergence-existing-edge}.
head: environment
name: Independence from the positive update weights

label: rem:single-edge-inheritance
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:single-edge-inheritance}
Suppose that the update consists of a single edge. Thus,
\(p=1\), \(B=b\in\mathbb R^n\), and
\(\Omega=[\omega]\) with \(\omega>0\), so that
\[
L_{G+H}=L_G+\omega bb^T.
\]
If
\(
\lambda\in\sigma(L_G)\cap\sigma(L_{G+H}),
\)
then necessarily
\(
\mathcal U_\lambda\neq\{0\},
\)
as we show next.
Hence, under a single positive edge update, every preserved eigenvalue
has a nonzero inherited eigenvector. This does not rule out the
simultaneous presence of emergent eigenvectors; it only shows that
a preserved eigenvalue cannot be preserved solely through emergence.

To see this, suppose, to the contrary, that
\(\mathcal U_\lambda=\{0\}\).
Choose any nonzero vectors
\(
x\in E_\lambda(L_G),
\) and \(
y\in E_\lambda(L_{G+H}).
\)
By Theorem~\ref{thm:inherited-eigenspace},
\(
\mathcal U_\lambda
=
E_\lambda(L_G)\cap\ker(b^T),
\)
so \(b^Tx\neq0\).
Since \(y\in E_\lambda(L_{G+H})\), we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:eigenvalueeq}
(L_G-\lambda I_n)y
=
-\omega b(b^Ty).
\end{equation}
Because \(L_G\) is symmetric and \(x\in E_\lambda(L_G)\),
\(
x^T(L_G-\lambda I_n)
=
\bigl((L_G-\lambda I_n)x\bigr)^T
=
0.
\)
Multiplying \eqref{eq:eigenvalueeq} on the left by \(x^T\)
therefore gives
\[
0=-\omega(x^Tb)(b^Ty).
\]
Since \(\omega>0\) and \(x^Tb\neq0\), it follows that
\(b^Ty=0\).
Substituting this into \eqref{eq:eigenvalueeq} yields
\(
(L_G-\lambda I_n)y=0.
\)
Thus,
\[
0\neq y\in E_\lambda(L_G)\cap\ker(b^T)
=\mathcal U_\lambda,
\]
a contradiction.
Therefore, \(\mathcal U_\lambda\neq\{0\}\).
In particular, preservation solely through emergence requires at least
two updated edges.
head: environment
name: Eigenvalue preservation under a single-edge update always involves inheritance

label: rem:inheritance-geometric-interpretation
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:inheritance-geometric-interpretation}
Let \(b_1,\ldots,b_p\) be the columns of \(B\), and recall that
\(P_\lambda=Q_\lambda Q_\lambda^T\) is the orthogonal projector onto
\(E_\lambda(L_G)\). The vectors \(Q_\lambda^Tb_\ell\) are the coordinates of
\(P_\lambda b_\ell\) with respect to the orthonormal basis formed by the
columns of \(Q_\lambda\). Hence,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:projected-edge-rank}
\operatorname{rank}(B^TQ_\lambda)=\operatorname{rank}(Q_{\lambda}^TB)=
\dim\left(
\operatorname{span}
\{Q_{\lambda}^Tb_1,\ldots,Q_{\lambda}^Tb_p\}
\right)
=
\dim\operatorname{span}
\{P_\lambda b_1,\ldots,P_\lambda b_p\}.
\end{equation}
If \(y\in E_\lambda(L_G)\), then \(P_\lambda y=y\). Since
\(P_\lambda\) is symmetric,
\(
b_\ell^Ty
=
b_\ell^TP_\lambda y
=
\left(P_\lambda b_\ell\right)^Ty
\). Therefore,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:inherited-geometric-description}
\mathcal U_\lambda=E_{\lambda}(L_G)\cap \ker(B^T)
=
E_\lambda(L_G)\cap
\operatorname{span}
\{P_\lambda b_1,\ldots,P_\lambda b_p\}^{\perp}.
\end{equation}
Thus, \(\operatorname{rank}(B^TQ_\lambda)\) is the codimension of the inherited subspace
inside \(E_\lambda(L_G)\). In other words, it is the number of independent directions removed from the original $\lambda$-eigenspace by the update.
In particular, \(\lambda\) is preserved through inheritance if and only if
the projected update-edge vectors do not span \(E_\lambda(L_G)\).
head: environment
name: Geometric interpretation

label: th1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{th1}
Let $L_G$ and $L_{G+H}=L_G+X_{\Omega}X_{\Omega}^{T}$ be the Laplacian matrices of $G$ and of an
updated graph of $G$, respectively. 
Let
\(\lambda\in\sigma(L_G)\cap\sigma(L_{G+H})\). Suppose that
\(
E_\mu(L_G)\subseteq E_\mu(L_{G+H})
\)
for every \(\mu\in\sigma(L_G)\) with \(\mu<\lambda\). Then 
\(
E_\lambda(L_{G+H})=\mathcal U_\lambda.
\)
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that $0$ is the smallest eigenvalue of $L_G$ and $L_{G+H}$. 
If $\lambda=0$,  we set $S=S'=\emptyset$. We use the convention that any vector is orthogonal to the empty set. 
For $\lambda >0$, define
\[
S:=\bigoplus_{\substack{\mu\in\sigma(L_{G})\\\mu<\lambda}}E_{\mu}(L_{G})\qquad\text{and}\qquad S^{\prime}:=\bigoplus_{\substack{\nu\in\sigma
(L_{G+H})\\\nu<\lambda}}E_{\nu}(L_{G+H}).
\]
Note that  $S\subseteq S^{\prime}$. Let $y$ be a unit vector in
$E_{\lambda}(L_{G+H})$ and let $C=X_{\Omega}X_{\Omega}^{T}$. Since $L_{G+H}$ is symmetric, we have $y\perp S^{\prime}$,
and therefore $y\perp S$. Then,\[
\lambda=\min_{x\bot S\text{,}\left\Vert x\right\Vert _{2}=1}(x^{T}L_Gx)\leq
y^{T}L_{G}y.
\]
Therefore,
\[
y^{T}L_{G}y+y^{T}Cy=y^{T}L_{G+H}y=\lambda\leq y^{T}L_{G}y.
\]
Since $C$ is positive semidefinite, we obtain $y^{T}Cy=0$. Since
$y^{T}Cy=\Vert X_{\Omega}^{T}y\Vert_{2}^{2}$, we have $X_{\Omega}^{T}y=0$.
Consequently,
\[
L_{G}y=L_{G+H}y-X_{\Omega}X_{\Omega}^{T}y=\lambda y.
\]
Thus $y\in E_{\lambda}(L_{G})$.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Let $L_G$ and $L_{G+H}=L_G+X_{\Omega}X_{\Omega}^{T}$ be the Laplacian matrices of $G$ and of an
updated graph of $G$, respectively. If $\lambda$ is one of the two smallest
eigenvalues (counting multiplicities) of $L_G$ and $\lambda\in\sigma(L_{G+H})$, then any $\lambda
$-eigenvector of $L_{G+H}$ is inherited.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If \(\lambda=0\), there are no eigenvalues of \(L_G\) smaller than
\(\lambda\). Thus, the hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{th1} is vacuously
satisfied, and the result follows.

Suppose now that \(\lambda\) is the second smallest eigenvalue of \(L_G\)
and that \(\lambda>0\). Then \(G\) is connected, so
\(
E_0(L_G)=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{1}\}.
\)
Since adding edges preserves connectivity, \(G+H\) is also connected, and
therefore
\(
E_0(L_{G+H})=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{1}\}.
\)
Thus, \(E_0(L_G)\subseteq E_0(L_{G+H})\). Since \(0\) is the only
eigenvalue of \(L_G\) smaller than \(\lambda\), the result follows from
Theorem~\ref{th1}.

title: Corollary
body_md: \label{cor:preliminary-updated-multiplicity} Let \(\lambda\in\sigma(L_G)\) and let \(Q_\lambda\) have orthonormal columns spanning \(E_\lambda(L_G)\). Then \begin{equation} \label{eq:preliminary-updated-multiplicity} m_\lambda(L_{G+H}) = \dim\mathcal U_\lambda + \dim\mathcal S_{\lambda,\Omega} = m_\lambda(L_G) - \operatorname{rank}(B^TQ_\lambda) + \dim\mathcal S_{\lambda,\Omega}. \end{equation}
head: environment
name: A preliminary multiplicity identity

title: Proof
body_md: Taking dimensions in \eqref{eq:inherited-emergent-decomposition} gives \[ m_\lambda(L_{G+H}) = \dim\mathcal U_\lambda + \dim \Phi_{\lambda,\Omega}(\mathcal S_{\lambda,\Omega}). \] The function  \(\Phi_{\lambda,\Omega}\)  is an isomorphism  with domain $\mathcal{S}_{\lambda, \Omega}$. Hence, \(\dim  \Phi_{\lambda,\Omega}(\mathcal S_{\lambda, \Omega})=\dim\mathcal S_{\lambda,\Omega}\). The final equality follows from Corollary~\ref{cor:inherited-dimension}.
head: environment

label: eq:secular-determinant-identity
title: Remark
body_md:
The matrix $F_\lambda(\Omega)$ is closely related to the classical
secular matrix for low-rank eigenvalue updates. If
$t\notin\sigma(L_G)$, the matrix determinant lemma gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:secular-determinant-identity}
\det(L_{G+H}-tI_n)
=
\det(L_G-tI_n)\det(\Omega)
\det\left(
\Omega^{-1}+B^T(L_G-tI_n)^{-1}B
\right).
\end{equation}
The $p\times p$ matrix
\[
\Omega^{-1}+B^T(L_G-tI_n)^{-1}B
\]
is the secular matrix. Since $Q_\lambda^TBZ=0$, its singular part at
$t=\lambda$ vanishes after multiplication by $Z^T$ and $Z$. Therefore,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:F-as-compressed-secular-limit}
F_\lambda(\Omega)
=
\lim_{t\to\lambda}
Z^T\left(
\Omega^{-1}+B^T(L_G-tI_n)^{-1}B
\right)Z.
\end{equation}
Thus, $F_\lambda(\Omega)$ is the limit of the secular matrix after
restricting it to $\mathcal K_\lambda$.
head: environment

label: prop:edge-difference-space
title: Theorem
body_md: \label{prop:edge-difference-space} With the notation above, \begin{equation} \label{eq:rescaled-edge-space-characterization} \mathcal Z_{\lambda,\Omega} = \left\{ z\in\mathcal K_\lambda: \bigl(\Omega^{-1}+\Gamma_\lambda\bigr)z \in\operatorname{range}(B^TQ_\lambda) \right\} = \left\{ Zc:c\in\ker F_\lambda(\Omega) \right\}. \end{equation}
head: environment
name: Characterization of the rescaled edge-difference space

label: eq:reduced-reconstruction-relations
title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(z\in\mathcal Z_{\lambda,\Omega}\). By definition \eqref{def:ZlambdaOmega}, there exists
\(y\in E_\lambda(L_{G+H})\) such that \(z=\Omega B^Ty\). The eigenvalue
equation $L_{G+H}y= \lambda y$ can therefore be written as
\(
(L_G-\lambda I_n)y+Bz=0.
\)
Multiplying by \(Q_\lambda^T\) on the left gives \(Q_\lambda^TBz=0\), so
\(z\in\mathcal K_\lambda\).

Write \(y=Q_\lambda a+r\), where $a=Q_{\lambda}^Ty$ and
\(r\in E_\lambda(L_G)^\perp\). Then
\((L_G-\lambda I_n)r=-Bz\). Since \(z\in\mathcal K_\lambda=\ker(Q_{\lambda}^TB)\), the vector
\(Bz\) belongs to \(E_\lambda(L_G)^\perp\), and hence
\(
r=-G_\lambda Bz.
\)
Thus,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:reduced-reconstruction-relations}
y=Q_\lambda a-G_\lambda Bz.
\end{equation}
Multiplying \eqref{eq:reduced-reconstruction-relations} by \(B^T\) and
using \(B^Ty=\Omega^{-1}z\) and
\(\Gamma_\lambda=B^TG_\lambda B\), we obtain
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:compatibility-condition}
B^TQ_\lambda a
=
(\Omega^{-1}+\Gamma_\lambda)z.
\end{equation}
Therefore,
\((\Omega^{-1}+\Gamma_\lambda)z\in
\operatorname{range}(B^TQ_\lambda)\).

Conversely, suppose that \(z\in\mathcal K_\lambda\) and
\(
(\Omega^{-1}+\Gamma_\lambda)z
\in\operatorname{range}(B^TQ_\lambda).
\)
Choose \(a\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfying
\eqref{eq:compatibility-condition}, and define \(y\) by
\eqref{eq:reduced-reconstruction-relations}. Then
\(B^Ty=\Omega^{-1}z\), so \(\Omega B^Ty=z\). Moreover, since $Q_{\lambda}^TBz=0$,
\[
(L_{G+H}-\lambda I_n)y
=
-P_{\lambda,\perp}Bz+Bz
=
P_\lambda Bz
=
0.
\]
Hence,
\(y\in E_\lambda(L_{G+H})\), and therefore
\(z\in\mathcal Z_{\lambda,\Omega}\). This completes the proof of the first equality in
\eqref{eq:rescaled-edge-space-characterization}.

Finally,
\(\operatorname{range}(B^TQ_\lambda)=\mathcal K_\lambda^\perp\).
Also, every \(z\in\mathcal K_\lambda\) can be written uniquely as
\(z=Zc\) for some $c\in \mathbb{R}^d$. Moreover,
\[
(\Omega^{-1}+\Gamma_\lambda)Zc\in\mathcal K_\lambda^\perp
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
Z^T(\Omega^{-1}+\Gamma_\lambda)Zc=0.
\]
By the definition of \(F_\lambda(\Omega)\), the last condition is
\(F_\lambda(\Omega)c=0\), which proves the second equality.

label: cor:weighted-algebraic-multiplicity
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Multiplicity after a positive edge update

label: thm:explicit-reconstruction
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Reconstruction of the canonical emergent subspace

title: Proof
body_md:
($\supseteq$) Let \(c\in\ker F_\lambda(\Omega)\). We  show that
\(y_c\in\mathcal C_{\lambda,\Omega}\).
By \eqref{eq:yc-zc}, $\Omega B^Ty_c=z_c$.  By definition of $Z$, $z_c:=Zc\in \mathcal{K}_{\lambda}$, and hence \(Q_\lambda^TBz_c=0\).
Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
(L_{G+H}-\lambda I_n)y_c
&=
(L_G-\lambda I_n)
\bigl(Q_\lambda a_c-G_\lambda Bz_c\bigr)
+Bz_c\\
&=
-P_{\lambda,\perp}Bz_c+Bz_c
=
P_\lambda Bz_c
=
0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, \(y_c\in E_\lambda(L_{G+H})\).

It remains to show that $y_c\perp\mathcal U_\lambda$. Since $a_c$ is
the minimum-norm solution of \eqref{eq:compatibility-eq}, $a_c\in\ker(B^TQ_\lambda)^\perp$.
Since $\mathcal U_\lambda
=
\left\{
Q_\lambda h:h\in\ker(B^TQ_\lambda)
\right\}$ by Theorem \ref{thm:inherited-eigenspace}, it follows that $Q_\lambda a_c\perp\mathcal U_\lambda$. Moreover,
$G_\lambda Bz_c\in \operatorname{range}({G_{\lambda}})=E_\lambda(L_G)^\perp$, while
$\mathcal U_\lambda\subseteq E_\lambda(L_G)$. Hence,
$G_\lambda Bz_c\perp\mathcal U_\lambda$. Therefore,
\[
y_c
=
Q_\lambda a_c-G_\lambda Bz_c
\perp\mathcal U_\lambda.
\]
Thus, $y_c\in\mathcal C_{\lambda,\Omega}$.

($\subseteq$) Let \(y\in\mathcal C_{\lambda,\Omega}\), and set
\(z:=\Omega B^Ty\). Then, by \eqref{def:ZlambdaOmega},
\(z\in\mathcal Z_{\lambda,\Omega}\), so
Theorem~\ref{prop:edge-difference-space} gives
\(z=Zc=z_c\) for a unique \(c\in\ker F_\lambda(\Omega)\). By \eqref{eq:yc-zc}, we have
\(\Omega B^Ty=\Omega B^Ty_c\). Because \(\Omega\) is invertible,
\(B^T(y-y_c)=0\). Moreover,
\(y-y_c\in E_\lambda(L_{G+H})\) because, by the first part of the proof, $y_c\in \mathcal{C}_{\lambda, \Omega}$. Hence,
\[
y-y_c\in
E_\lambda(L_{G+H})\cap\ker(B^T)
=
\mathcal U_\lambda.
\]
On the other hand,
\(y-y_c\in\mathcal U_\lambda^\perp\), because both \(y\) and \(y_c\)
belong to \(\mathcal C_{\lambda,\Omega}\). Therefore \(y-y_c=0\), and
hence \(y=y_c\).
This proves \eqref{eq:canonical-emergent-reconstruction}.
head: environment

label: cor:basis-updated-eigenspace
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: A basis of the updated eigenspace

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem~\ref{thm:inherited-eigenspace},
\(
\mathcal U_\lambda
=
\{Q_\lambda h:h\in\ker(B^TQ_\lambda)\}.
\)
Since $Q_{\lambda}$ has full column rank, $\{Q_\lambda h_1,\ldots,Q_\lambda h_s\}$ is a basis of $\mathcal{U}_{\lambda}.$

To prove the second part, we first note that the map \(c\mapsto y_c\) is linear. It is also injective. Indeed,  if $y_c=0$, then \eqref{eq:yc-zc} gives $Zc =0$. Since $Z$ has full column rank, $c=0.$
Moreover,
Theorem~\ref{thm:explicit-reconstruction} shows that the range of this
map is $\mathcal C_{\lambda,\Omega}$. Therefore, $\{y_{c_1},\ldots,y_{c_r}\}$ is a basis of $\mathcal C_{\lambda,\Omega}$.

Now the result follows since
\(
E_\lambda(L_{G+H})
=
\mathcal U_\lambda
\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}
\mathcal C_{\lambda,\Omega}.
\)
head: environment

label: ex:weighted-emergent-dimension
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:weighted-emergent-dimension} Let \(G\) be the path on three vertices, with Laplacian \[ L_G= \begin{pmatrix} 1&-1&0\\ -1&2&-1\\ 0&-1&1 \end{pmatrix}. \] The eigenvalues of \(L_G\) are \(0,1,3\), and the unit vector \(q=\frac1{\sqrt6}(1,-2,1)^T\) spans \(E_3(L_G)\). Add the missing edge \(\{1,3\}\) with weight \(\omega>0\). Thus, \(B=b=e_1-e_3\), \(\Omega=[\omega]\), and \(L_{G+H}=L_G+\omega bb^T\). Since \(q^Tb=0\), \(\mathcal K_3=\mathbb R\), and we may take \(Z=[1]\). The vector \(b\) is a \(1\)-eigenvector of \(L_G\), so
\((L_G-3I_3)b=-2b\). Since \(L_G\) is symmetric,
\(b\perp E_3(L_G)\). On \(E_3(L_G)^\perp\), the pseudoinverse
\(G_3=(L_G-3I_3)^\dagger\) agrees with the inverse of the restriction of
\(L_G-3I_3\). Hence, \(G_3b=-\frac12b\).

Since \(b^Tb=2\), it follows that
\(\Gamma_3=b^TG_3b=-1\). Therefore, the reduced matrix is given by \[ F_3(\Omega)=\left[\frac1{\omega}-1\right]\in \mathbb{R}^{1\times 1}. \] 
By Corollary~\ref{cor:weighted-algebraic-multiplicity}, an emergent
\(3\)-eigendirection occurs precisely when
\(\ker F_3(\Omega)\neq\{0\}\), or equivalently, when
\(F_3(\Omega)\) is singular. Since \(F_3(\Omega)\) is a \(1\times1\)
matrix, this happens precisely when
\(\omega=1\).
Since \(b^Tq=0\), Theorem~\ref{thm:inherited-eigenspace} shows that the original 3-eigenvector
\(q\) is inherited  for every \(\omega>0\).
Corollary~\ref{cor:weighted-algebraic-multiplicity} therefore gives \[ m_3(L_{G+H}) = \begin{cases} 1,&\omega\neq1,\\ 2,&\omega=1. \end{cases} \] 

We now use the reconstruction formula to obtain $\mathcal{C}_{3, \Omega}$ when $\omega=1$. In this case, we have \(\ker F_3(\Omega)=\mathbb R\). For 
\(c\in\mathbb R\), we have \(z_c=c\). Moreover, since
\(B^TQ_3=b^Tq=0\), the minimum-norm solution in
\eqref{eq:ac} is \(a_c=0\). Hence,
\[
y_c=-G_3bc=\frac{c}{2}b.
\]
Thus, every nonzero \(c\) produces the same canonical emergent direction,
and Theorem~\ref{thm:explicit-reconstruction} gives
\[
\mathcal C_{3,\Omega}
=
\operatorname{span}\{b\}.
\]

 Consequently, \begin{equation} \label{eq:P3-reduced-eigenspace} E_3(L_{G+H}) = \begin{cases} \operatorname{span}\{q\}, &\omega\neq1,\\[1mm] \operatorname{span}\{q\} \mathbin{\oplus^\perp} \operatorname{span}\{b\}, &\omega=1. \end{cases} \end{equation} 

This conclusion can also be checked directly: \(L_{G+H} b=(1+2\omega)b\). Thus, \(b\) becomes a \(3\)-eigenvector precisely when \(\omega=1\). At this exceptional weight, the added edge turns the path into a cycle, whose nonzero Laplacian eigenvalue \(3\) has multiplicity two.
head: environment
name: The reduced matrix for a one-edge update

label: def:exceptional-weight
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:exceptional-weight}
A positive diagonal matrix \(\Omega\) is called \emph{exceptional for
\(\lambda\)} if
$
\mathcal C_{\lambda,\Omega}\neq\{0\}.
$
The diagonal of an exceptional \(\Omega\) is called a \emph{vector of  exceptional weights}, or \emph{exceptional weights} when the context is clear.
head: environment

label: prop:existence-exceptional-weights
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{prop:existence-exceptional-weights}  Fix $L_G$, $\lambda \in \sigma(L_G)$ and $B$. Suppose that \(d>0\). Then  the following statements are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item[\rm(i)] There is a positive diagonal matrix $\Omega$ exceptional for $\lambda.$
\item[\rm(ii)] The symmetric matrix \(M_\lambda\) has a negative eigenvalue. \item[\rm(iii)] There exists \(\omega>0\) such that \(\omega I_p\) is exceptional for \(\lambda\). \end{enumerate} Moreover, for every \(\omega>0\), \begin{equation} \label{eq:equal-weight-emergent-dimension} \dim\mathcal C_{\lambda,\omega I_p} = \dim E_{-1/\omega}(M_\lambda). \end{equation} Consequently, $\omega I_p$ is exceptional if and only if $-1/\omega$ is a negative eigenvalue of $M_\lambda$. 
In particular, there are at most $d$ exceptional equal weights.
head: environment
name: Existence of exceptional weights

title: Proof
body_md:
We first show that (i) implies (ii). Assume that \(\Omega\) is exceptional. Then, by Theorem \ref{thm:explicit-reconstruction}, there exists a nonzero vector \(c\) such that \( F_\lambda(\Omega)c=0\). By \eqref{eq:F-weight-decomposition}, \[ c^TM_\lambda c = -c^TZ^T\Omega^{-1}Zc <0. \] 
The inequality is strict because \(\Omega^{-1}\) is positive definite and \(Zc\neq0\). Hence, since $M_{\lambda}$ is symmetric,  it follows that this matrix has a negative eigenvalue. 

We next show that (ii) implies (iii).  Suppose that \(M_\lambda c=\rho c\) for some \(c\neq0\) and \(\rho<0\). Set \(\omega=-1/\rho\). Since \(Z^TZ=I_d\), we have \(F_\lambda(\omega I_p)=\omega^{-1}I_d+M_\lambda\), and therefore \(F_\lambda(\omega I_p)c=0\). Thus, \(\omega I_p\) is exceptional,  by Theorem \ref{thm:explicit-reconstruction}. 

The implication from (iii) to (i) is immediate. 

Finally, let \(\omega>0\). By Theorem~\ref{thm:explicit-reconstruction},
\(
\dim \mathcal C_{\lambda,\omega I_p}
=
\dim\ker F_\lambda(\omega I_p).
\)
Since
\(
F_\lambda(\omega I_p)
=
\omega^{-1}I_d+M_\lambda,
\)
we have
\[
\ker F_\lambda(\omega I_p)
=
\ker\bigl(M_\lambda+\omega^{-1}I_d\bigr)
=
E_{-1/\omega}(M_\lambda).
\]
Therefore,
\[
\dim\mathcal C_{\lambda,\omega I_p}
=
\dim E_{-1/\omega}(M_\lambda),
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:equal-weight-emergent-dimension}.

It follows that $\omega I_p$ is exceptional if and only if $E_{-1/\omega}(M_\lambda)\neq\{0\}$ or, equivalently, if and only if $-1/\omega$ is an eigenvalue of $M_\lambda$. 
Since $\omega>0$, this eigenvalue is negative. 
Thus, each exceptional equal weight $\omega=-1/\rho$ is determined by a negative eigenvalue $\rho$ of $M_\lambda$.
Since $M_\lambda$ is a $d\times d$ matrix, there are at most $d$ such exceptional  weights.
head: environment

label: prop:fixed-relative-weights
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:fixed-relative-weights}
 Fix $L_G$, $\lambda \in \sigma(L_G)$ and $B$. Suppose that $d>0$, and let $\Omega_0$ be a fixed positive diagonal matrix. 
Then there exists a positive diagonal matrix $\Omega$ exceptional for $\lambda$ if and only if $t\Omega_0$ is exceptional for some $t>0$.
Moreover, $t\Omega_0$ is exceptional if and only if $-1/t$ is a negative eigenvalue of
$$
\widetilde M_{\lambda,\Omega_0}
=
T_0^{-1/2}M_\lambda T_0^{-1/2},
\qquad
T_0=Z^T\Omega_0^{-1}Z.
$$
In particular, there are at most $d\leq p$ exceptional positive scale factors $t$.
head: environment
name: Fixed relative update weights

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $Z$ has full column rank and $\Omega_0$ is positive diagonal, $T_0$ is positive definite. 
Hence,
$$
F_\lambda(t\Omega_0)
=
t^{-1}T_0+M_\lambda
=
T_0^{1/2}
\left(
t^{-1}I_d+\widetilde M_{\lambda,\Omega_0}
\right)
T_0^{1/2}.
$$
Taking into account that $T_0^{1/2}$ is invertible, by Corollary~\ref{cor:basis-updated-eigenspace},
$$
\dim\mathcal C_{\lambda,t\Omega_0}
=
\dim\ker F_\lambda(t\Omega_0)
=
\dim\ker
\left(
t^{-1}I_d+\widetilde M_{\lambda,\Omega_0}
\right)
=
\dim E_{-1/t}
\bigl(\widetilde M_{\lambda,\Omega_0}\bigr).
$$

Therefore, $t\Omega_0$ is exceptional for $\lambda$ if and only if $-1/t$ is a negative eigenvalue of $\widetilde M_{\lambda,\Omega_0}$.

Moreover, $\widetilde M_{\lambda,\Omega_0}$ is congruent to $M_\lambda$. 
By Sylvester's law of inertia, $\widetilde M_{\lambda,\Omega_0}$ has a negative eigenvalue if and only if $M_\lambda$ has a negative eigenvalue. 
By Theorem~\ref{prop:existence-exceptional-weights}, this holds if and only if some positive diagonal matrix $\Omega$ is exceptional for $\lambda$.

Finally, since $\widetilde M_{\lambda,\Omega_0}$ is a $d\times d$ matrix, there are at most $d\leq p$ exceptional positive scale factors $t$.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Fix $L_G$, $\lambda \in \sigma(L_G)$ and $B$. Assume that $\Omega$  is exceptional for $\lambda$.  Then $\lambda_{\min}(M_{\lambda})<0$ and 
$\omega_{\max}\geq 
-\frac{1}{\lambda_{\min}(M_\lambda)}$, where \(\omega_{\max}\) is the largest diagonal entry of
\(\Omega\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first claim follows immediately from Theorem \ref{prop:existence-exceptional-weights}. Now we prove the second claim. Since 
\(\Omega^{-1}\succeq \omega_{\max}^{-1}I_p\) and 
\(Z^TZ=I_d\),
\[
Z^T\Omega^{-1}Z
\succeq
\frac{1}{\omega_{\max}}I_d.
\]
Thus, by \eqref{eq:F-weight-decomposition}, we have
\[
F_\lambda(\Omega)
\succeq
\left(
\frac{1}{\omega_{\max}}
+
\lambda_{\min}(M_\lambda)
\right)I_d.
\]
Since $\Omega$ is exceptional for $\lambda$, $F_\lambda(\Omega)$ is singular by Corollary \ref{cor:weighted-algebraic-multiplicity}. 
Therefore, 
$$
\frac{1}{\omega_{\max}}
+
\lambda_{\min}(M_\lambda)
\leq 0,
$$
which completes the proof.
head: environment

label: cor:single-edge-exceptional-weight
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:single-edge-exceptional-weight}
Let $\lambda \in \sigma(L_G)$. Suppose that \(p=1\), and let \(b\) be the oriented update-edge vector.
An exceptional edge weight $\omega$ for $\lambda$ exists if and only if  \[Q_\lambda^Tb=0\quad \text{and} \quad
b^TG_\lambda b<0.
\]
In this case, the exceptional weight is unique and is given by
\[
\omega
=
-\frac{1}{b^TG_\lambda b}.
\]
head: environment
name: Single-edge updates

title: Proof
body_md:
If \(Q_\lambda^Tb\neq0\), then
\(\mathcal K_\lambda=\ker Q_{\lambda}^Tb=\{0\}\), and hence \(d=\dim \mathcal K_\lambda=0\) and  no exceptional weights exist. 

Suppose now that \(Q_\lambda^Tb=0\). Then
\(\mathcal K_\lambda=\mathbb R\), and we may take \(Z=[1]\). Thus,
\[
F_\lambda(\Omega)
=
\omega^{-1}+b^TG_\lambda b.
\]
By Theorem \ref{thm:explicit-reconstruction},  $\omega$ is exceptional for $\lambda$ if and only if $F_{\lambda}(\Omega)=0.$ Since $\omega>0$, this equation has a solution if and only if $b^TG_\lambda b<0$.
In this case, the solution is unique and is given by $\omega
=
-\frac{1}{b^TG_\lambda b}.
$
head: environment

label: lem:polynomial-exceptional-weights
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:polynomial-exceptional-weights}
The polynomial \(p_\lambda(s)\) is  not identically zero and is affine in each variable.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix all variables
except \(s_i\). Then there exists a matrix $A$ independent of $s_i$ such that
\[\widehat F_\lambda(s)=A+s_i\zeta_i\zeta_i^T, \qquad \zeta_i = Z^Te_i.\]
The rank-one determinant identity gives 
\[
\det(A+s_i\zeta_i\zeta_i^T)
=
\det(A)
+
s_i\zeta_i^T\operatorname{adj}(A)\zeta_i.
\]
Thus, for every $i$, \(p_\lambda\) is affine in \(s_i\). 

To show that $p_\lambda$ is not identically zero, set $s_1=\cdots=s_p=t$. Since $Z^TZ=I_d$,
$$
\widehat F_\lambda(t,\ldots,t)
=
tI_d+M_\lambda.
$$
Therefore,
$$
p_\lambda(t,\ldots,t)
=
\det(tI_d+M_\lambda),
$$
which is a monic polynomial of degree $d$. 
Hence, $p_\lambda$ is not identically zero.
head: environment

label: cor:one-weight-exceptional
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{cor:one-weight-exceptional}
Suppose that \(d>0\). 
Then a positive weight vector $(\omega_1, \ldots, \omega_p)$  is
exceptional for \(\lambda\) if and only if
\(p_\lambda(s_1, \ldots, s_p)=0\), where $s_i=1/\omega_i$.
Consequently, the set of  exceptional  weight vectors has 
Lebesgue measure zero in \((0,\infty)^p\).
head: environment
name: Polynomial characterization of the exceptional set

label: eqhatqlambda
title: Proof
body_md:
The first claim follows from the definition of \(p_\lambda\).
 By Lemma~\ref{lem:polynomial-exceptional-weights},
\(p_\lambda\) is a nonzero polynomial.
Clearing denominators in
\(p_\lambda(1/\omega_1,\ldots,1/\omega_p)\) and taking into account that $p_{\lambda}$ is affine in each variable, we get the nonzero
polynomial
\begin{equation}\label{eqhatqlambda}
\widehat{p}_\lambda(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_p)
:=
(\omega_1\cdots\omega_p)
p_\lambda\left(\frac{1}{\omega_1},\ldots,\frac{1}{\omega_p}\right).
\end{equation}
Thus, a positive
weight vector is exceptional if and only if it is a zero
of \(\widehat{p}_\lambda\).
The conclusion follows because the zero set of a nonzero
real polynomial has Lebesgue measure zero.
head: environment

label: rem:alternative-determinant
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:alternative-determinant}

The preceding theorem characterizes exceptional weights using
\(p_\lambda\), a polynomial in the reciprocal weights \(s_i\).
A polynomial characterization can also be obtained directly in the update
weights \(\omega_i\). A natural first attempt is to use
\[
\det\bigl(L_G-\lambda I_n+B\Omega B^T\bigr)
\]
for this purpose. If \(\mathcal U_\lambda\neq\{0\}\), however,
this determinant vanishes for every positive diagonal matrix
\(\Omega\), because every inherited vector belongs to the kernel of
\(L_G-\lambda I_n+B\Omega B^T\).
Thus, the full determinant does not distinguish emergence from
preservation through inheritance.

To remove the inherited subspace, let
\(h:=\dim\mathcal U_\lambda\), and choose
\(V\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-h)}\) with orthonormal columns spanning
\(\mathcal U_\lambda^\perp\). Since \(\mathcal U_\lambda\) is
independent of the positive update weights, \(V\) can also be
chosen independently of them. Define
\[
q_\lambda(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_p)
:=
\det\left(
V^T\bigl(L_G-\lambda I_n+B\Omega B^T\bigr)V
\right).
\]
When \(\mathcal U_\lambda=\{0\}\), we may take \(V=I_n\), so
\(q_\lambda\) reduces to the full determinant above. Since \(L_{G+H}-\lambda I_n\) is symmetric and vanishes
on \(\mathcal U_\lambda\), it leaves
\(\mathcal U_\lambda^\perp\) invariant. Consequently,
multiplication by \(V\) maps the kernel of
\(
V^T\bigl(L_G-\lambda I_n+B\Omega B^T\bigr)V
\)
isomorphically onto \(\mathcal C_{\lambda,\Omega}\). Hence,
\[
q_\lambda(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_p)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\Omega\text{ is exceptional for }\lambda.
\]

Moreover, \(q_\lambda\) and \(p_\lambda\) give the same polynomial description of the exceptional set, up to the reciprocal change of variables and a nonzero constant factor. More precisely,
\[
q_\lambda(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_p)
=
c_\lambda(\omega_1\cdots\omega_p)
p_\lambda\left(
\frac{1}{\omega_1},\ldots,\frac{1}{\omega_p}
\right),
\]
where \(c_\lambda\neq0\) is independent of the update weights. 
This identity is stronger than the fact that the two polynomials have the same positive zero set and does not follow from that fact alone. 
It can be proved by a block determinant calculation using orthonormal bases adapted to \(\mathcal U_\lambda\) and \(\mathcal K_\lambda\), together with Schur complements.

Since \(p_\lambda\) is nonzero, the identity shows that \(q_\lambda\) is also a nonzero polynomial.
Its positive zeros are precisely the exceptional weight vectors.

We work with \(p_\lambda\) because it arises from the reduced
matrix \(F_\lambda(\Omega)\), whose order is \(d\leq p\), compared
with \(n-h\) for the matrix defining \(q_\lambda\). Moreover,
\(F_\lambda(\Omega)\) is the same reduced matrix used to determine
emergence and its multiplicity and to reconstruct the canonical
emergent subspace. Its explicit dependence on the reciprocal
weights therefore provides a convenient unified framework for
the analysis in this section.
head: environment
name: An alternative determinant formulation

label: cor:fix-one-variable
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:fix-one-variable}
 Fix all update weights except one, say \(\omega_i\). Then the set of
positive values of \(\omega_i\) for which the resulting weight vector $(\omega_1, \ldots, \omega_p)$
is exceptional is empty, a singleton, or all of \((0,\infty)\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fixing all the weights except \(\omega_i\) is equivalent to fixing all
reciprocal variables except \(s_i=1/\omega_i\). 
By
Lemma~\ref{lem:polynomial-exceptional-weights},
\(p_\lambda\) is affine in \(s_i\), that is,
\(
p_\lambda(s)=as_i+b,
\)
where $a$ and $b$  are constant. Thus, the set of positive zeros of $p_{\lambda}(s)$  is empty, a singleton, or all of $(0,\infty)$. Since $s_i=1/\omega_i$ is a bijection from $(0,\infty)$ onto itself, the same holds for the exceptional values of $\omega_i$.
head: environment

label: ex:equal-unequal-exceptional-weights
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:equal-unequal-exceptional-weights} 
Consider the path on three vertices  with unit edge weights, and its Laplacian eigenvalue \(\lambda=3\). Increase the weights of the two existing edges \(\{1,2\}\) and \(\{2,3\}\) by \(\omega_1,\omega_2>0\), respectively. We can take
\[ B= \begin{bmatrix} 1&0\\ -1&1\\ 0&-1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \Omega=\operatorname{diag}(\omega_1,\omega_2). \] 
The vector \(q=\frac1{\sqrt6}(1,-2,1)^T\) spans \(E_3(L_G)\), and \(\mathcal K_3=\operatorname{span}\{(1,1)\}\). Taking \(Z=\frac1{\sqrt2}(1,1)^T\), one obtains 
\[ \Gamma_3 = -\frac14 \begin{bmatrix} 1&1\\ 1&1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad M_3=\left[-\frac12\right], \qquad F_3(\Omega) = \left[\frac12 \left( \frac1{\omega_1}+\frac1{\omega_2}-1 \right)\right]. \] 
Therefore, emergence occurs precisely when \begin{equation} \label{eq:P3-exceptional-weight-curve} \frac1{\omega_1}+\frac1{\omega_2}=1, \end{equation} 
or equivalently, 
$$s_1+s_2=1.$$

This equation has infinitely many positive solutions.  At every point on the exceptional curve, \(F_3(\Omega)=[0]\). Since \(F_3(\Omega)\) is \(1\times1\), it follows that \(\dim\ker F_3(\Omega)=1\). Hence \(\dim\mathcal C_{3,\Omega}=1\), and every exceptional weight vector produces exactly one canonical emergent direction.
 The unique exceptional equal weight is \(\omega_1=\omega_2=2\), in agreement with Theorem~\ref{prop:existence-exceptional-weights}. Moreover, since  \(B^Tq\neq0\), by Theorem \ref{thm:inherited-eigenspace},  no nonzero \(3\)-eigenvector is inherited.
head: environment

label: thm:higher-nullity-strata
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:higher-nullity-strata}
Let
\(
\Omega=\operatorname{diag}(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_p)
\)
be any positive diagonal matrix such that
\(\mathcal C_{\lambda,\Omega}\neq\{0\}\), and set
\(
s_0=
\left(
\frac1{\omega_1},\ldots,\frac1{\omega_p}
\right).
\)

Then, for every \(r\in\{2,\ldots,d\}\),
\(
\dim\mathcal C_{\lambda,\Omega}\geq r
\)
if and only if
\(
\partial_Jp_\lambda(s_0)=0
\)
for every subset \(J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}\) satisfying
\(
1\leq |J|\leq r-1.
\)

Moreover,
\(
\dim\mathcal C_{\lambda,\Omega}=1
\)
if and only if \(s_0\) is a regular point of the zero set of
\(p_\lambda\).
head: environment
name: Multiplicity of emergence at exceptional weights

label: derivatives of q
title: Proof
body_md:
By
Corollary~\ref{cor:basis-updated-eigenspace} and \eqref{widehatF},
\[
k:=\dim\ker \widehat F_\lambda(s_0)=\dim\mathcal C_{\lambda,\Omega}\geq1.
\]
In particular, \(p_\lambda(s_0)=\det \widehat F_\lambda(s_0)=0\).
For \(i=1,\ldots,p\), set \(\zeta_i:=Z^Te_i\).

Suppose that \(k\geq r\), and let
\(J=\{j_1,\ldots,j_m\}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}\) satisfy
\(1\leq m=|J|\leq r-1\).
Define the polynomial in the variables \(t_j\), \(j\in J\), by
\[
g_J(t):=
p_\lambda\left(s_0+\sum_{j\in J}t_je_j\right).
\]
We first show that \(g_J\) is identically zero.
By \eqref{widehatF}, for any scalars \(a_j\), $j\in J$,
\[
\widehat F_\lambda\left(s_0+\sum_{j\in J}a_je_j\right)
=
\widehat F_\lambda(s_0)+\sum_{j\in J}a_j\zeta_j\zeta_j^T.
\]
The rank--nullity theorem gives \(\operatorname{rank}\widehat F_\lambda(s_0)=d-k\). Also,
 each matrix \(a_j\zeta_j\zeta_j^T\) has rank at most one.
Since \(k\geq r>|J|\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{rank}\left(
\widehat F_\lambda(s_0)+\sum_{j\in J}a_j\zeta_j\zeta_j^T
\right)
\leq \operatorname{rank}\widehat F_\lambda(s_0)+|J|
=d-k+|J|<d.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, the matrix $\widehat F_\lambda(s_0)+\sum_{j\in J}a_j\zeta_j\zeta_j^T$ is singular for every choice of the scalars
\(a_j\), and therefore,
\[
g_J(t)
=
\det\left(\widehat F_\lambda(s_0)+\sum_{j\in J}t_j\zeta_j\zeta_j^T\right)
\equiv
0.
\]
Each variable \(t_j\) changes only the \(j\)th coordinate of
the argument of \(p_\lambda\). Hence, by the chain rule,
\[
\frac{\partial^{m}g_{J}}{\partial t_{j_{1}}\cdots\partial t_{j_{m}}}(t)=\frac{\partial^{m}p_{\lambda}}{\partial s_{j_{1}}\cdots\partial
s_{j_{m}}}\left(  s_{0}+\sum_{j\in J}t_{j}e_{j}\right)  .
\]
Thus, 
\[
0=\frac{\partial^{m}g_{J}}{\partial t_{j_{1}}\cdots\partial t_{j_{m}}}(0)=\frac{\partial^{m}p_{\lambda}}{\partial s_{j_{1}}\cdots\partial
s_{j_{m}}}(s_{0})=\partial_{J}p_{\lambda}(s_{0}),
\]
where the first equality holds because \(g_J\) is identically
zero. This proves the ``only if'' implication.

Conversely, suppose that \(\partial_Jp_\lambda(s_0)=0\) for
every \(J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}\) satisfying
\(1\leq|J|\leq r-1\).
Since the columns of \(Z\) are orthonormal,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^p\zeta_i\zeta_i^T
=
Z^T\left(\sum_{i=1}^pe_ie_i^T\right)Z
=
Z^TZ
=
I_d.
\]
Consequently, the polynomial, in the real variable $t$,
\(
q(t):=p_\lambda(s_0+t\mathbf1_p)
\)
satisfies
\[
q(t)
=
\det\left(\widehat F_\lambda(s_0)+t\sum_{i=1}^p\zeta_i\zeta_i^T\right)
=
\det(\widehat F_\lambda(s_0)+tI_d).
\]

Recall that \(p_\lambda\) is affine in each variable.
Thus, every partial derivative in which the same variable
is differentiated twice is zero.
Repeated application of the chain rule therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{derivatives of q}
q^{(\ell)}(0)
=
\ell!
\sum_{\substack{J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}\\|J|=\ell}}
\partial_Jp_\lambda(s_0),
\qquad 1\leq\ell\leq r-1.
\end{equation}
The factor \(\ell!\) accounts for the possible orders of
differentiation with respect to the \(\ell\) distinct variables
indexed by \(J\).
By assumption, every term in the sum is zero, so
\(q^{(\ell)}(0)=0\) for \(1\leq\ell\leq r-1\).
Since also \(q(0)=p_\lambda(s_0)=0\), we conclude that
\(q(t)\) is divisible by \(t^r\).

The matrix \(\widehat F_\lambda(s_0)\) is real symmetric and therefore has an
orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. Since \(\dim\ker \widehat F_\lambda(s_0)=k\),
exactly \(k\) of its eigenvalues are zero, counted with
multiplicity.
Let \(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_{d-k}\) be its nonzero eigenvalues,
also counted with multiplicity. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:qfactorization}
q(t)
=
\det(\widehat F_\lambda(s_0)+tI_d)
=
t^k\prod_{j=1}^{d-k}(\mu_j+t),
\end{equation}
where an empty product is understood to equal \(1\).
Since each \(\mu_j\neq0\), the product is nonzero at \(t=0\).
Thus, \(q(t)\) is divisible by \(t^k\) but not by \(t^{k+1}\).
Since it is also divisible by \(t^r\), we conclude that
\(k\geq r\),   proving the ``if'' claim.

For \(d\geq2\), the final assertion follows directly from the
equivalence just proved with \(r=2\), since \(k\geq1\) and $p_{\lambda}(s_0)=0.$

It remains to consider \(d=1\). In this case, \(1\leq k\leq d\)
implies \(k=1\), so \(\widehat F_\lambda(s_0)\) is the
\(1\times1\) zero matrix. Since \(Z^TZ=I_1\), we have
\[
q(t)=p_\lambda(s_0+t\mathbf1_p)
=
\det\bigl(\widehat F_\lambda(s_0)+tI_1\bigr)
=
t.
\]
Differentiating with respect to \(t\), evaluating at \(t=0\), and using \eqref{derivatives of q}
gives
\[
\sum_{i=1}^p
\frac{\partial p_\lambda}{\partial s_i}(s_0)
=
1.
\]
Thus, at least one first partial derivative is nonzero,
and \(s_0\) is a regular point of the zero set of \(p_\lambda\).
Since \(\dim\mathcal C_{\lambda,\Omega}=k=1\), the final
assertion also holds when \(d=1\).

body_md:
\label{ex:large-cycle-three-edges}
Let \(G\)  be the cycle on 1000 vertices with unit edge weights. Consider its Laplacian eigenvalue
\[
\lambda
=
2-2\cos\left(\frac{8\pi}{1000}\right)
\approx 6.316214334\times10^{-4}.
\]
The corresponding eigenspace has dimension two and is spanned by the vectors $u$ and $v$ whose
\(j\)th entries are
\[
u_j=\sqrt{\frac{2}{1000}}
\cos\left(\frac{8\pi(j-1)}{1000}\right)
\quad\text{and}\quad
v_j=\sqrt{\frac{2}{1000}}
\sin\left(\frac{8\pi(j-1)}{1000}\right).
\]
Let $Q_{\lambda}=[u, v].$ We add the three diameter edges
\[
\{1,501\},\qquad
\{101,601\},\qquad
\{201,701\},
\]
and let \(B\in\mathbb R^{1000\times3}\) contain their oriented edge
vectors. The entries of both \(\lambda\)-eigenvectors agree at the
endpoints of each update edge. Hence, \(Q_\lambda^TB=0\). Thus, \(\mathcal K_\lambda=\mathbb R^3\), and we take \(Z=I_3\). By
Theorem~\ref{thm:inherited-eigenspace}, the original two-dimensional
\(\lambda\)-eigenspace is inherited for every positive choice of the
three update weights. 

Let $b_i$ denote the $i$th column of $B$, as before. A computation gives
\[
b_i^TG_\lambda b_j
=
\frac{4}{1000}
\sum_{\substack{m=0\\m\ {\rm odd}}}^{999}
\frac{
\cos\!\left(
2\pi m(r_i-r_j)/1000
\right)
}{
\lambda_m-\lambda
},
\]
where \(r_1=0\), \(r_2=100\), \(r_3=200\), and
\(\lambda_m=2-2\cos(2\pi m/1000)\).
Evaluating these sums,  we obtain
\[
M_\lambda
=
\Gamma_\lambda
=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&-\alpha&\beta\\
-\alpha&0&-\alpha\\
\beta&-\alpha&0
\end{pmatrix},
\]
where
\[
\alpha
=
\frac{\sin(\pi/5)}{\sin(\pi/125)}
\approx23.3896943853,
\qquad
\beta
=
\frac{\sin(2\pi/5)}{\sin(\pi/125)}
\approx37.8453205018.
\]
Consequently, for
\(\Omega=\operatorname{diag}(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3)\),
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:large-cycle-reduced-matrix}
F_\lambda(\Omega)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\omega_1^{-1}&-\alpha&\beta\\
-\alpha&\omega_2^{-1}&-\alpha\\
\beta&-\alpha&\omega_3^{-1}
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
In the reciprocal variables \(s_i=1/\omega_i\), its determinant is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:large-cycle-exceptional-polynomial}
p_\lambda(s)
=
s_1s_2s_3
-\alpha^2(s_1+s_3)
-\beta^2s_2
+2\alpha^2\beta.
\end{equation}

This polynomial displays two features of the general theory. First, if we fix
\(s_1=s_3=\beta\), then
\(p_\lambda(s)=0\) for every \(s_2>0\) (recall Corollary \ref{cor:fix-one-variable}). By Theorem \ref{cor:one-weight-exceptional}, if
\[
\omega_1=\omega_3=\frac1\beta
\approx0.0264233461,
\]
then every positive value of \(\omega_2\) is exceptional. 
Now consider
\[
\begin{aligned}
s_*&=\left(\beta,\frac{\alpha^2}{\beta},\beta\right),\\
\Omega_*&=\operatorname{diag}
\left(\frac1\beta,\frac{\beta}{\alpha^2},\frac1\beta\right)\\
&\approx\operatorname{diag}
(0.0264233461,0.0691772181,0.0264233461).
\end{aligned}
\]
At this point,
\[
F_\lambda(\Omega_*)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\beta&-\alpha&\beta\\
-\alpha&\alpha^2/\beta&-\alpha\\
\beta&-\alpha&\beta
\end{pmatrix}
=
qq^T,
\qquad
q=
\begin{pmatrix}
\sqrt{\beta}\\
-\alpha/\sqrt{\beta}\\
\sqrt{\beta}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Therefore, \(F_\lambda(\Omega_*)\) has rank one and nullity two. Hence, by Corollary \ref{cor:basis-updated-eigenspace},
\(\dim\mathcal C_{\lambda,\Omega_*}=2\). Since the original
two-dimensional \(\lambda\)-eigenspace is inherited, the multiplicity of
\(\lambda\) in the updated Laplacian is four. 

Table~\ref{tab:large-cycle-weights} reports the dimension of $\mathcal{C}_{\lambda, \Omega}$ for  several graph updates $G+H$, three of which correspond to exceptional weight vectors. In each case, the multiplicity of $\lambda$ as an eigenvalue of $L_{G+H}$ is obtained by adding $2= \dim(\mathcal{U}_{\lambda})$ to the dimension of $\mathcal{C}_{\lambda, \Omega}.$ 
For this purpose, we computed
the kernel of the \(3\times 3\) matrix \(F_\lambda(\Omega)\). We note that the term \(M_\lambda\), which involves the computation of the pseudoinverse of a $1000\times 1000$ matrix, needs to be computed only once, since it is independent of $\Omega.$ Then,  many choices of
the three update weights can be tested without repeatedly computing the relevant eigenspace of the
\(1000\times1000\) updated Laplacian.

The exceptional $\Omega$'s with equal diagonal entries appearing in Table~\ref{tab:large-cycle-weights} are obtained from the two negative eigenvalues
of \(M_\lambda\), according to Theorem \ref{prop:existence-exceptional-weights}.
